More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

Footage shows a major landslide cascading down a steep mountainside in Darchula, northwestern Nepal. Authorities fear it may block the Chameliya River and have warned riverside residents to remain alert over the risk of further blockage and sudden flooding.

Nepal Flood and Major Health Risks On August 26, 2026, a massive flash flood swept through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system after a sudden surge of water, ice, rock, and mud from the Himalayan border region. The disaster destroyed communities, roads, bridges, homes, water systems, and hydropower facilities. As of September 4, more than 1,250 people had been reported dead and over 4,200 were still missing, while thousands of people had been displaced from their homes. The destruction has turned the flood from an immediate natural disaster into a serious public-health crisis. (Reuters) One of the biggest health concerns is unsafe drinking water. Flooding damaged water-supply and sanitation systems, which can allow sewage, waste, and other contamination to enter water used for drinking and cooking. UNICEF reports that at least 22,000 children urgently need clean water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance. This creates a greater risk of diarrheal and other waterborne illnesses, especially among young children. (UNICEF) Another major concern is the spread of infectious disease in crowded shelters and temporary housing. Many displaced families are staying together in holding centers or with other households, making respiratory infections easier to spread. Standing water and disrupted sanitation may also increase the risk of mosquito- and other vector-borne diseases. WHO is additionally concerned about contaminated food, infected wounds, injuries caused by debris, and shortages of essential medical care. (World Health Organization) The flood has also damaged Nepal’s ability to provide healthcare. WHO reports that three health posts were completely damaged, one hospital was partially damaged, and access to two other hospitals was affected. This means people may struggle to receive emergency treatment as well as regular care such as medications, maternal care, treatment for chronic diseases, and other essential health services. (World Health Organization) Finally, survivors may face important mental-health effects, including grief, trauma, fear, and stress after losing relatives, homes, or livelihoods. Nepal’s immediate challenge is therefore not only rescuing survivors but also providing clean water, sanitation, food, shelter, medical treatment, disease monitoring, and functioning healthcare services. If these needs are addressed quickly, many illnesses and additional deaths after the flood can be prevented. (World Health Organization) #nepal #floods #nepaltibet #safety
